source.title: Deep Neural Networks as Gaussian Processes
source.authors: Jaehoon Lee; Yasaman Bahri; Roman Novak; S. Schoenholz; Jeffrey Pennington; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein

record.tranche_reason: Reports training classification accuracy for gradient-trained networks on CIFAR-10, but uses fully connected networks rather than the convolutional networks in V1.
record.gate_note: Figure 2 includes networks filtered for 100% classification training accuracy; the paper does not report how many runs were trained before filtering. Other reported accuracy and MSE results are test-set results and do not bear on the claim's training-error outcome.
record.test_reason: The study's own results do not test any listed version. R1 and R2 describe fully connected networks selected for perfect training accuracy, whereas V1 specifies convolutional networks. The initialization and depth experiments measure Bayesian NNGP test performance, not gradient-based learning speed or trainable depth under V4. Statements about initialization enabling deeper gradient-trained networks are attributed to prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases Figure 2, provided it remains restricted to networks selected for perfect training accuracy. The paper's broader conclusion is that deep infinite-width fully connected network priors correspond to Gaussian processes, enabling exact Bayesian regression, and that optimized finite-network test performance approaches NNGP performance as width increases.
record.recipe_differences: Uses fully connected networks with five hidden layers, cross-entropy loss, and random optimization and initialization hyperparameters; the claim version names convolutional networks and also includes CIFAR-100 and corrupted or random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The Figure 2 analysis is conditioned on nonlinearity and filters networks by 100% classification training accuracy; the paper reports separate aggregate counts for Tanh and ReLU.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 analyzes 125 Tanh and 55 ReLU fully connected networks selected for 100% training classification accuracy; the widest selected networks generalize best.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Among five-hidden-layer fully connected networks selected for perfect CIFAR-10 training accuracy, the widest networks have the smallest generalization gaps.

fits_no_version.finding: NNGP test accuracy is best near signal-propagation criticality, with a narrower favorable hyperparameter region as kernel depth increases; sufficiently degenerate kernels lose useful information through numerical precision.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight and bias prior variances near signal-propagation criticality preserve useful deep NNGP kernels for Bayesian prediction.

record.problems: Figure 2 reports only networks selected for 100% classification training accuracy; the text does not give the total number of runs before filtering, so success frequency cannot be determined.
record.rows_left_out: Test accuracy, test MSE, and generalization-gap results were omitted because they do not measure training classification error. Other reported NNGP results concern Bayesian predictions rather than gradient-based training outcomes.

untested.parts: Training classification error in convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, including corrupted or random labels and the effects of model size, early stopping and regularization.
Spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Training-error degradation with depth in plain convolutional networks, identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization exceptions.
Effects of initialization on gradient-based learning speed and trainable depth, including orthogonal versus Gaussian weights and very deep plain convolutional networks.
Loss recovery, curvature evolution and divergence relative to learning-rate stability thresholds.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and the Fixup comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Section 3.1 describes training 180 networks, while Figure 2 reports 180 networks after filtering. This wording does not clearly establish an unfiltered denominator or a success rate. Generalization, test-performance and Bayesian-prediction results are already declared in rows_left_out and require no missing-result entries.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, convolutional networks, and the frequency of reaching zero training error across all runs.

rows.subject: five hidden layer fully-connected networks (Tanh; aggregate of 125 networks)
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with random optimization and initialization hyperparameters; reported results were filtered for 100% classification training accuracy.
rows.note: The paper reports 125 Tanh networks after filtering; it does not state the number of networks trained before filtering.
rows.check: The 100% training accuracy is a selection criterion for the generalization-gap analysis, not an independently reported optimization outcome. These are fully connected Tanh networks, outside V1's convolutional-network scope. The selected count of 125 does not establish optimization success frequency.
